claims.text: Selective dealloying of a noble-metal-based HEA precursor containing a less-noble sacrificial element can produce a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting three-dimensional nanoframework has enhanced catalytic properties.
The precursor is a homogeneous HEA composed primarily of noble metals and one or more less-noble sacrificial metals.
Chemical dealloying, such as acid etching, selectively removes the sacrificial element from the HEA precursor.
Appropriate control of temperature, acid concentration, and treatment time permits selective removal while preserving the multimetal HEA framework.
Removal of sacrificial components forms an interconnected porous network containing nanoscale ligaments and voids.
The nanoscale ligaments and voids expose active catalytic sites.
Selective etching of less-stable elements prompts the remaining noble-metal atoms to self-assemble into a three-dimensional nanoframework.
Dealloying increases the surface area of the HEA.
Dealloying enhances atomic-scale mixing among the remaining metals.
Increased surface area and enhanced atomic-scale mixing collectively improve catalytic performance.
The dealloyed HEA will have a higher BET surface area than the starting bulk HEA.
The dealloyed HEA will expose more catalytically active noble-metal sites than the starting bulk HEA.
The dealloyed HEA will exhibit greater catalytic activity than the starting bulk HEA.
Untreated bulk HEAs typically have lower surface areas and fewer accessible active sites than dealloyed HEA nanoframeworks.
Overly aggressive etching can collapse the porous structure.
Insufficiently aggressive etching may fail to create adequate porosity.
The method may be limited to HEAs whose constituent elements differ sufficiently in electrochemical stability.
Increased porosity and atomic order provide a strong rationale for enhanced catalysis.
The optimal dealloying parameters and long-term operating stability of the nanoframework remain unvalidated.
